description: Akira ransomware, written in C++, is most prominently (but not exclusively) associated with the ransomware-as-a-service entity Akira. Akira ransomware has been used in attacks across North America, Europe, and Australia, with a focus on critical infrastructure sectors including manufacturing, education, and IT services. Akira ransomware employs hybrid encryption and threading to increase the speed and efficiency of encryption and runtime arguments for tailored attacks. Notable variants include Rust-based Megazord for targeting Windows and Akira _v2 for targeting VMware ESXi servers.

ref-67f4298eafcd169b076f.text: MultiLayer Wiper uses a batch script to clear file system cache memory via the ProcessIdleTasks export in advapi32.dll as an anti-analysis and anti-forensics technique. MultiLayer Wiper reboots the infected system following wiping and related tasks to prevent system recovery. MultiLayer Wiper wipes the boot sector of infected systems to inhibit system recovery. MultiLayer Wiper changes timestamps of overwritten files to either 1601.1.1 for NTFS filesystems, or 1980.1.1 for all other filesystems. MultiLayer Wiper changes the original path information of deleted files to make recovery efforts more difficult. MultiLayer Wiper uses a batch script launched via a scheduled task to delete Windows Event Logs. MultiLayer Wiper opens a handle to \\\\\\\\.\\\\PhysicalDrive0 and wipes the first 512 bytes of data from this location, removing the boot sector. MultiLayer Wiper deletes files on network drives, but corrupts and overwrites with random data files stored locally. BFG Agonizer wipes the boot sector of infected machines to inhibit system recovery. BFG Agonizer uses DLL unhooking to remove user mode inline hooks that security solutions often implement. BFG Agonizer also uses IAT unhooking to remove user-mode IAT hooks that security solutions also use. MultiLayer Wiper contains two binaries in its resources section, MultiList and MultiWip. MultiLayer Wiper drops and executes each of these items when run, then deletes them after execution. MultiLayer Wiper generates a list of all files and paths on the fixed drives of an infected system, enumerating all files on the system except specific folders defined in a hardcoded list. MultiLayer Wiper removes Windows event logs during execution. MultiLayer Wiper removes the Volume Shadow Copy (VSS) service from infected devices along with all present shadow copies. MultiLayer Wiper creates a malicious scheduled task that launches a batch file to remove Windows Event Logs. BFG Agonizer retrieves a device handle to \\\\.\\PhysicalDrive0 to wipe the boot sector of a given disk. BFG Agonizer uses elevated privileges to call NtRaiseHardError to induce a "blue screen of death" on infected systems, causing a system crash. Once shut down, the system is no longer bootable. MultiLayer Wiper uses a batch file, remover.bat to delete malware artifacts and the batch file itself during execution.
ref-67f4298eafcd169b076f.title: Or Chechik, Tom Fakterman, Daniel Frank & Assaf Dahan. (2023, November 6). Agonizing Serpens (Aka Agrius) Targeting the Israeli Higher Education and Tech Sectors. Retrieved May 22, 2024.

ref-7653549f67c3522aa042.text: Olympic Destroyer will attempt to enumerate mapped network shares to later attempt to wipe all files on those shares. Olympic Destroyer uses the native Windows utilities vssadmin, wbadmin, and bcdedit to delete and disable operating system recovery features such as the Windows backup catalog and Windows Automatic Repair. Olympic Destroyer attempts to copy itself to remote machines on the network. Olympic Destroyer uses API calls to enumerate the infected system's ARP table. Olympic Destroyer contains a module that tries to obtain credentials from LSASS, similar to Mimikatz. These credentials are used with PsExec and Windows Management Instrumentation to help the malware propagate itself across a network. Olympic Destroyer will shut down the compromised system after it is done modifying system configuration settings. Olympic Destroyer will attempt to clear the System and Security event logs using wevtutil. Olympic Destroyer contains a module that tries to obtain stored credentials from web browsers. Olympic Destroyer uses WMI to help propagate itself across a network. Olympic Destroyer uses the API call ChangeServiceConfigW to disable all services on the affected system. Olympic Destroyer utilizes PsExec to help propagate itself across a network. Olympic Destroyer uses Windows Management Instrumentation to enumerate all systems in the network. Olympic Destroyer overwrites files locally and on remote shares.
ref-7653549f67c3522aa042.title: Mercer, W. and Rascagneres, P. (2018, February 12). Olympic Destroyer Takes Aim At Winter Olympics. Retrieved March 14, 2019.

ref-897a16438f630de6b729.text: SynAck can manipulate Registry keys. SynAck enumerates Registry keys associated with event logs. SynAck payloads are obfuscated prior to compilation to inhibit analysis and/or reverse engineering. SynAck encrypts the victims machine followed by asking the victim to pay a ransom. SynAck checks its directory location in an attempt to avoid launching in a sandbox. SynAck enumerates all running processes. SynAck enumerates all running services. SynAck parses the export tables of system DLLs to locate and call various Windows API functions. SynAck gathers user names from infected hosts. SynAck lists all the keyboard layouts installed on the victim’s system using GetKeyboardLayoutList API and checks against a hardcoded language code list. If a match if found, SynAck sleeps for 300 seconds and then exits without encrypting files. SynAck gathers computer names, OS version info, and also checks installed keyboard layouts to estimate if it has been launched from a certain list of countries. SynAck abuses NTFS transactions to launch and conceal malicious processes. SynAck clears event logs.
ref-897a16438f630de6b729.title: Ivanov, A. et al. (2018, May 7). SynAck targeted ransomware uses the Doppelgänging technique. Retrieved May 22, 2018.

ref-96bc5ab42e4b38546123.text: The Akira _v2 encryptor targets the `/vmfs/volumes/` path by default and can use the rust-crypto 0.2.36 library crate for the encryption processes. Akira can encrypt victim filesystems for financial extortion purposes including through the use of the ChaCha20 and ChaCha8 stream ciphers. Akira _v2 can enumerate the trace, debug, error, info, and warning logs on targeted systems. Akira _v2 can stop running virtual machines. Akira _v2 can target specific files and folders for encryption. Akira _v2 will fail to execute if the targeted `/vmfs/volumes/` path does not exist or is not defined. Megazord can encrypt files on targeted Windows hosts leaving them with a ".powerranges" file extension. Akira examines files prior to encryption to determine if they meet requirements for encryption and can be encrypted by the ransomware. These checks are performed through native Windows functions such as GetFileAttributesW.
ref-96bc5ab42e4b38546123.title: Nutland, J. and Szeliga, M. (2024, October 21). Akira ransomware continues to evolve. Retrieved December 10, 2024.

ref-ba036217b9af5c3654a0.text: WannaCry utilizes wmic to delete shadow copies. WannaCry uses vssadmin, wbadmin, bcdedit, and wmic to delete and disable operating system recovery features. WannaCry creates the service "mssecsvc2.0" with the display name "Microsoft Security Center (2.0) Service." WannaCry uses attrib +h and icacls . /grant Everyone:F /T /C /Q to make some of its files hidden and grant all users full access controls. WannaCry uses an exploit in SMBv1 to spread itself to other remote systems on a network. WannaCry enumerates current remote desktop sessions and tries to execute the malware on each session. WannaCry searches for variety of user files by file extension before encrypting them using RSA and AES, including Office, PDF, image, audio, video, source code, archive/compression format, and key and certificate files. WannaCry encrypts user files and demands that a ransom be paid in Bitcoin to decrypt those files. WannaCry attempts to copy itself to remote computers after gaining access via an SMB exploit.
ref-ba036217b9af5c3654a0.title: Noerenberg, E., Costis, A., and Quist, N. (2017, May 16). A Technical Analysis of WannaCry Ransomware. Retrieved December 8, 2024.

ref-bc0367492d7779c139e0.text: DarkGate tries to elevate privileges to SYSTEM using PsExec to locally execute as a service, such as cmd /c c:\temp\PsExec.exe -accepteula -j -d -s [Target Binary]. DarkGate use Nirsoft Network Password Recovery or NetPass tools to steal stored RDP credentials in some malware versions. DarkGate relies on parent PID spoofing as part of its "rootkit-like" functionality to evade detection via Task Manager or Process Explorer. DarkGate includes one infection vector that leverages a malicious "KeyScramblerE.DLL" library that will load during the execution of the legitimate KeyScrambler application. DarkGate masquerades malicious LNK files as PDF objects using the double extension .pdf.lnk. DarkGate is distributed in phishing emails containing links to distribute malicious VBS or MSI files. DarkGate uses applications such as Microsoft Teams for distributing links to payloads. DarkGate command and control includes hard-coded domains in the malware masquerading as legitimate services such as Akamai CDN or Amazon Web Services. DarkGate checks the BeingDebugged flag in the PEB structure during execution to identify if the malware is being debugged. DarkGate command and control includes hard-coded domains in the malware chosen to masquerade as legitimate services such as Akamai CDN or Amazon Web Services. DarkGate executes a Windows Batch script during installation that creases a randomly-named directory in the C:\\ root directory that copies and renames the legitimate Windows curl command to this new location. DarkGate uses per-victim links for hosting malicious archives, such as ZIP files, in services such as SharePoint to prevent other entities from retrieving them. DarkGate uses a hard-coded string as a seed, along with the victim machine hardware identifier and input text, to generate a unique string used as an internal mutex value to evade static detection based on mutexes.
ref-bc0367492d7779c139e0.title: Ernesto Fernández Provecho, Pham Duy Phuc, Ciana Driscoll & Vinoo Thomas. (2023, November 21). The Continued Evolution of the DarkGate Malware-as-a-Service. Retrieved February 9, 2024.

ref-c225923fbd0926257059.text:
BlackByte Ransomware gathers victim system information to generate a unique victim identifier.
BlackByte Ransomware is distributed as an obfuscated JavaScript launcher file.
BlackByte Ransomware checks for files related to known sandboxes.
BlackByte Ransomware is distributed as a JavaScript launcher file.
BlackByte Ransomware uses the `mountvol.exe` command to mount volume names and leverages the Microsoft Discretionary Access Control List tool, `icacls.exe`, to grant the group to “Everyone” full access to the root of the drive.
BlackByte Ransomware enables SMBv1 during execution.
BlackByte Ransomware modifies the victim Registry to prevent system recovery.
BlackByte Ransomware looks for security software products prior to full execution.
BlackByte Ransomware uses mapped shared folders to transfer ransomware payloads via SMB.
BlackByte Ransomware creates a mutex value with a hard-coded name, and terminates if that mutex already exists on the victim system. BlackByte Ransomware checks the system language to see if it matches one of a list of hard-coded values; if a match is found, the malware will terminate.
BlackByte Ransomware enumerates the Registry, specifically the `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options` key.
BlackByte Ransomware spreads itself laterally by writing the JavaScript launcher file to mapped shared folders.
BlackByte Ransomware deletes all volume shadow copies and restore points among other actions to inhibit system recovery following ransomware deployment.
BlackByte Ransomware is ransomware using a shared key across victims for encryption.
BlackByte Ransomware uses the `SetThreadExecutionState` API to prevent the victim system from entering sleep.
BlackByte Ransomware is distributed as an encrypted payload.
BlackByte Ransomware adds .JS and .EXE extensions to the Microsoft Defender exclusion list. BlackByte Ransomware terminates and removes the Raccine anti-ransomware utility.
BlackByte Ransomware identifies the language on the victim system.
BlackByte Ransomware can identify network shares connected to the victim machine.
BlackByte Ransomware identifies remote systems via active directory queries for hostnames prior to launching remote ransomware payloads.
BlackByte Ransomware creates a schedule task to execute remotely deployed ransomware payloads.
ref-c225923fbd0926257059.title: Rodel Mendrez & Lloyd Macrohon. (2021, October 15). BlackByte Ransomware – Pt. 1 In-depth Analysis. Retrieved December 16, 2024.

ref-d9981b65d682273e80b6.text:
LockBit 3.0 can use code packing to hinder analysis.
LockBit 3.0 has the ability to directly call native Windows API items during execution.
ref-d9981b65d682273e80b6.title: INCIBE-CERT. (2024, March 14). LockBit: response and recovery actions. Retrieved February 5, 2025.

ref-f570a61cea2557a560b6.text:
Megazord can ignore specified directories for encryption.
Megazord has the ability to terminate a list of services and processes.
Megazord has the ability to print the trace, debug, error, info, and warning logs.
Megazord can execute multiple commands post infection via `cmd.exe`.
Megazord can terminate a list of specified services and processes.
ref-f570a61cea2557a560b6.title: Zemah, Y. (2024, December 2). Threat Assessment: Howling Scorpius (Akira Ransomware). Retrieved January 8, 2025.

ref-f97735853534cb303a48.text: Akira will leverage COM objects accessed through WMI during execution to evade detection. Akira executes native Windows functions such as GetFileAttributesW and `GetSystemInfo`. Akira verifies the deletion of volume shadow copies by checking for the existence of the process ID related to the process created to delete these items. Akira can identify remote file shares for encryption. Akira executes from the Windows command line and can take various arguments for execution. Akira uses the GetSystemInfo Windows function to determine the number of processors on a victim machine.
ref-f97735853534cb303a48.title: Max Kersten & Alexandre Mundo. (2023, November 29). Akira Ransomware. Retrieved April 4, 2024.
